newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 9.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BTR SET TO SLASH DIVIDEND AND LAUNCH SHAKE-UP

The conglomerate BTR is set to announce a cut in dividend, a restructuring of boardroom responsibilities and a disposal programme to raise two billion stg. The dividend cut is forecast by analysts to be between 30 and 40 per cent and will be announced on Thursday along with an expected fall of up to 15 per cent to 600 million stg in underlying profits. The market's reception of BTR chief executive Ian Strachan's reforms will be crucial in determining whether BTR receives 220 million stg from warrants which become exercisable after the interim figures are announced.
-- BRITISH MIDLAND DIGS IN OVER SLOTS

British Midland is ready to resist pressure to surrender take-off and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport as part of an Anglo-American transatlantic air pact designed to pave the way for an alliance between British Airways and American Airlines. Richard Branson, owner of Virgin, said the British Airways offer to reduce slots was a last-minute attempt to offset Office of Fair Trading concerns that the alliance is uncompetitive.
-- FLEXTECH AHEAD IN RACE FOR BBC DEAL

Talks between the BBC and Flextech, which owns and maintains a number of pay-TV channels, have gathered pace. It is believed Flextech has the edge over British Sky Broadcasting in negotiating the joint venture with the corporation. Sir Christopher Bland, chairman of BBC, is believed to have been contacted by head of Tele-Communications, the largest cable company in America and 51 per cent owner of Flextech, John Malone, to assure him of his company's support for the deal.
THE TIMES
-- PLANNERS TARGET EMPTY OFFICES FOR EXTRA LONDON HOUSING

In order to provide for the huge increase in demand for accommodation in London boroughs are being urged to convert acres of flats and houses. These proposals could mean a quadrupling of housing density in certain areas and a sharp reduction in provision for motor cars. A report is being sent to 32 boroughs from the London Planning Advisory Committee that would make more dwellings available to accommodate an anticipated 420,000 additional households in the next decade.
-- DEUTSCHE TO SACK KEY FUND CHIEFS

Morgan Grenfell, the investment bank, has promised to pay compensation to investors in three funds whose trading was suspended last week after investigations by financial regulators. Compensation could amount to tens of millions stg. This pledge is part of a programme by Morgan Grenfell's owner Deutsche Bank to restore public confidence. Deutsche has made it clear that it will demand the resignation of five or more senior managers at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management as soon as an investigation by Deutsche and the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation is completed in a month or so.
-- EXCHANGE ON THE TRAIL OF TWO BIG INSIDER DEALING RINGS

Two major insider-dealing rings which are believed to have syphoned millions of stg of illegal profits from the market are being investigated by officials of the London Stock Exchange. The exchange's director of market services, Richard Kilsby, and Stuart Paul-Clarke, head of surveillance, are leading the campaign against the suspected rings to sharpen the exchange's attack on market abuse with a powerful real-time computer monitoring system.
THE GUARDIAN
-- JERSEY POLITICIANS CLASH OVER ACCOUNTANCY LAW

A row has broken out in Jersey over legislation which would give accountancy partnerships limited liability status and protect them from having to make huge compensation payments to unhappy clients. The legislation is the first of its kind in Europe and, if passed, two of Britain's biggest accountancy firms, Price Waterhouse and Ernst and Young, would move their global head offices to Jersey. The matter caused a row in Jersey's parliament when Stuart Syvret, one of the island's two Green Party senators, was suspended for making allegations about the way the legislation has been framed.
-- BRITISH GAS LOOKS READY FOR A GRILLING

Analysts want to know how the British Gas board intends to counter the regulatory wrangles, demerger plans and contract negotiations with gas producers which beset it. On Thursday the main issue will be whether British Gas will reject the regulator's final price proposals and request a reference to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
-- REVIVAL BYPASSES CORNER SHOP

A report from Verdict Research predicts that more than one in 10 of Britain's corner shops will go out of business in the next five years because of increased competition from supermarkets. The survey says that small retailers specialising in confectionery, tobacco and news sales are losing the competitive advantage they traditionally enjoyed from their low cost base.
THE INDEPENDENT
- FUND MAY NOT PLAY BY GREENBURY'S RULES

Mercury Asset Management (MAM), the City's biggest pension fund manager, has told clients that it is prepared to ignore the Cadbury and Greenbury rulebooks on corporate governance whenever it is in the "economic interest" of shareholders to do so. MAM has issued a plea for flexibility in interpreting the rules in a four-page statement of principles of corporate governance which emerged atg the weekend, the first time it has set out its views on how directors should run their companies.
-- HYDRO SUED FOR 25 MILLION STG

Hydro-Electric, the Scottish electricity company, is being sued for 25 million stg by a small specialist energy consultancy which alleges it reneged on a joint-venture deal and poached a key member of staff. A writ was served last month by Sterling Energy Equities UK and the Court of Session in Edinburgh has given the plaintiffs leave to proceed with the claim. The case will centre around a five-year agreement which Hydro and Sterling entered into in 1994 and which was terminated last October. Sterling allege Hydro "enticed away" one of its project team.
-- PRINCIPAL HOTELS TO FLOAT THIS AUTUMN

The UK operator of period hotels, Principal Hotels, is to seek a stock market listing later this autumn which will value the company at around 100 million stg. Principal has 21 hotels and in 1994 Principal chairman John Lewis led a management buy-in of the group. Since then 11 million stg has been spent on improving existing sites.
